cards.title: One Currency, Many Countries
cards.definition: The euro is a single currency shared by a group of European Union members called the euro area or eurozone. Each country keeps its own government, budget and taxes, but gives up its own currency and interest rate. Monetary policy for the whole area is set centrally, so the same interest rate applies whether a member's economy is booming or shrinking.
cards.example: The euro was launched on 1 January 1999 for accounting and electronic payments, and notes and coins followed on 1 January 2002. By 2026, 21 of the 27 EU countries used it, with Bulgaria the latest to join, and some 358 million people paid with euro cash every day.

cards.title: The Eurosystem
cards.definition: The European System of Central Banks is the European Central Bank plus the national central banks of every EU member, whether or not it uses the euro. The Eurosystem is the smaller group: the ECB plus the national central banks of euro countries. The Eurosystem runs the single monetary policy, with the ECB at its core and national banks carrying out operations locally.
cards.example: The ECB has set monetary policy for the euro area since January 1999. Eleven countries started; Greece joined in 2001, Slovenia in 2007, Cyprus and Malta in 2008, Slovakia in 2009, Estonia in 2011, Latvia in 2014, Lithuania in 2015, Croatia in 2023 and Bulgaria in 2026.

cards.title: The Rules for Joining
cards.definition: Before a country can adopt the euro it must meet convergence criteria written into the EU Treaty. The idea is that economies sharing one interest rate should already look alike: low inflation, sound public finances, a stable exchange rate and long-term interest rates close to the best performers. The criteria are tested when a country applies for membership, not enforced afterwards, which is one reason the tests are strict.
cards.example: The tests: inflation no more than 1.5 percentage points above the average of the 3 lowest-inflation members; a government deficit within 3 percent of GDP and debt within 60 percent of GDP; at least 2 years in the exchange rate mechanism without devaluing; and long-term rates no more than 2 percentage points above the 3 best performers.

cards.title: Price Stability at 2 Percent
cards.definition: The Treaty makes price stability the ECB's primary objective but does not define it. The ECB does. After its 2021 strategy review it set a target of 2 percent inflation over the medium term and made the target symmetric, meaning undershooting is as unwelcome as overshooting. The target applies to the euro area as a whole, not to each member separately.
cards.example: The Governing Council adopted the 2 percent symmetric target in July 2021. It measures inflation with the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, a basket built the same way in every member so that a 2 percent reading in one country means the same as in another. Medium term means the ECB does not react to every month's wobble.

cards.definition: A flash estimate is an early reading of inflation published within days of the month's end, before all the data are in. It breaks the headline into components: energy, food, industrial goods and services. Watching the pieces matters because a jump driven by energy can reverse quickly, while services inflation tends to move slowly and reflects wages. The full figure follows about two weeks later.

cards.title: Government Debt in a Currency Union
cards.definition: Euro members share a currency but each issues its own government debt and has its own budget; there is no common treasury standing behind them. That is why debt ratios matter so much in the euro area: a member with heavy debt cannot print its way out, and its bonds trade at rates that reflect its own finances rather than the bloc's.

Greece stood at 143.5 percent, Italy 138.9 percent and France 117.6 percent; Estonia was lowest at 25.2 percent. cards.definition: Joining the euro means converting a national currency at a rate fixed irrevocably; the old currency then ceases to exist. Unlike a peg, which a government can abandon under pressure, the conversion rate has no exit. That permanence is what gives the union credibility, and also why the convergence tests come before entry: once in, a country can no longer devalue.

cards.title: China's Economy in 2025
cards.definition: China measures its output the way other countries do, as gross domestic product, and publishes a preliminary annual figure in January. Growth is reported in real terms, after removing price changes, against the same period a year earlier. Because the quarterly readings are year-on-year, a slowing quarterly sequence within a year signals a loss of momentum even when the annual total looks steady.
cards.example: GDP in 2025 was 140,187.9 billion yuan, about 140.2 trillion yuan, up 5.0 percent on 2024, according to the preliminary accounting released January 21, 2026. The quarters slowed through the year: 5.4 percent, 5.2 percent, 4.8 percent and 4.5 percent year on year.

cards.title: Four Decades of Catch-up
cards.definition: Economic reform in China began in 1978, opening the economy to markets and trade. The result was one of the fastest sustained expansions on record, which moved the country through the World Bank's income groups and pulled hundreds of millions of people above the extreme poverty line. The pace has slowed as the population ages and the easy gains from moving farm workers into factories have been taken.
cards.example: GDP growth averaged more than 9 percent a year from 1978 into the 2020s, and almost 800 million people were lifted out of extreme poverty. China moved from the low-income group to the upper-middle-income group. The World Bank's 2026 update projected growth easing to 4.4 percent in 2026 as aging and weaker demand weigh.

cards.title: A Population That Is Shrinking
cards.definition: A population shrinks when deaths outnumber births and migration does not fill the gap. For an economy that means fewer new workers each year and more retirees per worker, which weighs on growth and public finances. Urbanization, the share of people living in cities, can still rise even as the total falls, because people keep moving from countryside to town.
cards.example: At the end of 2025 China's population was 1,404.89 million, down 3.39 million over the year, with 7.92 million births against 11.31 million deaths. The urbanization rate rose 0.89 percentage points to 67.89 percent, according to the statistical communiqué of February 28, 2026.

cards.title: Three Sectors

As economies mature, services grow fastest and take the largest share. China's figures show that shift under way, with construction, long a growth engine, contracting even as services expanded. Watching the three sectors separately shows where growth is actually coming from, which a single GDP number hides.

Comparing the two with consumer prices shows whether living standards are rising: if income grows faster than prices, real purchasing power increases. A flat price index means every yuan of extra income was real.

cards.title: A Managed Float
cards.definition: A managed floating exchange rate lets the currency move with market supply and demand inside limits set by the central bank. China's version references a basket of currencies rather than the U.S. dollar alone, and the central bank publishes a daily central parity around which trading may move within a band. It is neither a hard peg nor a free float.
cards.example: China unified its dual exchange rates on January 1, 1994 and on July 21, 2005 moved to a managed float based on market supply and demand with reference to a basket of currencies. The daily band against the dollar was 0.3 percent at the 2005 reform and was widened to 0.5 percent in 2007.

cards.title: Tools of the People's Bank
cards.definition: The People's Bank of China steers credit with several levers. The required reserve ratio sets how much of their deposits banks must park at the central bank; cutting it frees money to lend. The 7-day reverse repo rate is the short-term policy rate. The loan prime rate is the benchmark banks quote to their best customers, and it guides mortgage and business loan pricing.

cards.definition: Total GDP and GDP per person tell different stories. A country can have the second-largest economy in the world and still have an average income well below that of rich countries, simply because the output is shared among many more people. Per capita figures are what matter for living standards; totals are what matter for the country's weight in world trade and finance.

cards.title: What "Emerging Market" Means
cards.definition: There is no single official definition of an emerging market. The phrase usually means a middle-income economy that is growing and opening to trade and investment but whose financial markets are smaller and less developed than those of rich countries. The World Bank avoids the label and instead sorts every economy into 4 income groups by national income per person.
cards.example: The World Bank groups economies as low, lower-middle, upper-middle or high income using gross national income per capita converted with its Atlas method, updated every July 1. cards.title: Extreme Poverty
cards.definition: Extreme poverty is living below an international poverty line that the World Bank sets in purchasing-power terms, so that a dollar buys the same basket in every country. The line is revised as price data improve. Falling poverty in East and South Asia drove most of the decline since 1990; what remains is concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and in places affected by conflict.
cards.example: The international line is $3.00 a day at 2021 purchasing-power parity. In the World Bank's 2025 estimates about 831 million people lived below it, down from roughly 2.3 billion in 1990. An estimated 412 million children aged 17 or under lived in such households in 2024, and progress has slowed over the past decade.

cards.title: Remittances
cards.definition: Remittances are money that migrants send home to family. For many developing countries they are a larger and steadier source of foreign currency than investment by foreign firms or aid from governments, because migrants keep sending even when the home economy is weak. The cost of sending money matters: every percentage point of fees is income that never arrives, which is why lowering that cost is a development goal in itself.
cards.example: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries reached $669 billion in 2023, up 3.8 percent, and exceeded foreign direct investment and official aid combined. The largest recipients were India at $125 billion, Mexico $67 billion, China $50 billion, the Philippines $40 billion and Egypt $24 billion. Sending $200 cost 6.2 percent on average in the second quarter of 2023.

cards.definition: Foreign direct investment is money a company puts into a lasting stake abroad: a factory, a mine, a subsidiary. It brings capital, technology and jobs and is harder to withdraw than a bond or a bank loan. Headline totals can mislead, because some flows merely pass through low-tax conduit economies on their way elsewhere without building anything, so analysts strip those out.

cards.title: Borrowing in Someone Else's Currency
cards.definition: When a country borrows in a foreign currency at a floating interest rate, it takes on two risks it cannot control: the lender's central bank can raise rates, and its own currency can fall, making each repayment cost more at home. In the 1970s banks recycled oil exporters' surplus dollars into loans to Latin America on exactly those terms, and cheap real rates made the debt seem manageable.
cards.example: Latin American debt rose from $29 billion in 1970 to $159 billion in 1978 and $327 billion in 1982. When the United States tightened money to fight inflation, rates jumped and repayment periods shortened. In August 1982 Mexico announced it could not service its $80 billion debt; 16 Latin American countries and 11 others went on to reschedule.

cards.title: The Lost Decade and the Brady Plan
cards.definition: A debt crisis becomes a lost decade when the cure, austerity to keep paying, chokes growth for years. Debt reduction breaks the cycle by writing part of the debt off in exchange for new bonds the borrower can service. Lenders accept a loss because a smaller debt that gets paid is worth more than a larger one that does not. Regulators first had to be sure the banks could absorb the write-offs.
cards.example: By 1982 the 9 largest U.S. banks held Latin American debt equal to 176 percent of their capital. The years 1982 to 1989 brought high unemployment, falling incomes per person and stagnant growth. The Brady plan of 1989 offered permanent relief: between 1989 and 1994 private lenders forgave $61 billion, about one-third of the debt.

cards.title: When a Peg Breaks: Asia, 1997
cards.definition: A currency peg fixes the exchange rate to the dollar. It invites firms and banks to borrow in dollars, often short term, because the rate seems guaranteed. If foreign lenders lose confidence and pull out, the central bank runs short of reserves and the peg breaks. The currency falls, and every dollar debt suddenly costs far more in local money, pushing borrowers into insolvency.

Firms saw the local value of their foreign debts jump. cards.title: Spillovers to the Rest of the World
cards.definition: A crisis in emerging markets travels along two channels. Trade: collapsing demand and cheaper currencies mean cheaper exports, which lowers prices elsewhere. Finance: investors flee to the safest assets, usually U.S. Treasury bonds, pushing their yields down. So the same shock that devastates the crisis countries can arrive in rich economies as lower inflation and cheaper borrowing, at least at first.

topics.summary: How prices, private property, competition, and business entry and exit coordinate a market economy, and what the record shows when competition or prices are suspended.

cards.title: What a Market Economy Is
cards.definition: A market economy is a system in which individuals and private businesses own most resources - land, labor, and capital - and decide how to use them through voluntary exchanges in markets. Government plays a comparatively small role. Two forces do most of the coordinating: self-interest, which motivates people to produce and trade, and competition, which restrains what any one seller can charge or get away with. No central office decides what, how, or for whom to produce.
cards.example: A loaf of bread reaches a shelf through at least 5 separate businesses - a farm, a mill, a bakery, a trucking firm, and a grocer - none of them instructed by a bread ministry. Each acts for its own gain, yet the chain delivers the loaf. In a 2005 lecture in Adam Smith's hometown of Kirkcaldy, the Federal Reserve chairman recalled Smith's point that we get our dinner not from the baker's benevolence but from his regard for his own interest, guided by an 'invisible hand'.

cards.title: Prices as Signals
cards.definition: In a market economy a price does two jobs at once. It is a signal: a rising price tells buyers and sellers that a good has become scarcer relative to the demand for it. It is also an incentive: the same rise nudges buyers to use less and sellers to supply more. When the quantity supplied equals the quantity demanded, the price is at its market-clearing level; a price above that produces a surplus, and a price below it produces a shortage.
cards.example: The St. Louis Fed's 2013 essay uses airline baggage. When carriers began charging $20 to $25 for a first checked bag, passengers checked fewer bags and carried more aboard. Overhead bins then filled up - a shortage of a good that was still free - and some airlines responded by charging for carry-on bags too. The fee was information, not just revenue.

cards.title: Property Rights and Titles
cards.definition: Markets need clear ownership. A property right is an enforceable claim to use an asset, to exclude others from it, and to sell it. A title is the legal record of that claim. When ownership is secure, people build, plant, and lend against what they hold, because they expect to keep the return. Where title is uncertain or easily overridden, that investment shrinks. Much of what governments do in market economies is record and enforce who owns what.
cards.example: The Homestead Act of 1862 turned public land into private titles. A settler could claim 160 acres, live on and farm it for 5 years, and then own it outright for a small fee, or buy it sooner at $1.25 an acre. Of some 500 million acres the government dispersed between 1862 and 1904, about 80 million went to homesteaders; most went to speculators, railroads, and other large holders.

cards.title: Competition and Antitrust
cards.definition: Competition is the regulator of a market economy: a seller who overcharges or cuts quality loses customers to rivals. Antitrust law exists for the cases where that check fails. It bans agreements among competitors to fix prices, divide markets, or rig bids, and it lets courts block mergers and practices that would leave one firm able to raise prices without losing business. The aim is to protect the process of competition itself, not any particular competitor.
cards.example: Congress passed the Sherman Act in 1890 and added the Clayton Act and the Federal Trade Commission Act in 1914; those 3 laws remain the core of U.S. antitrust. The Sherman Act is also a criminal statute: as published by the FTC, a corporation can be fined up to $100 million and an individual up to $1 million and 10 years in prison for fixing prices or rigging bids.

cards.title: Regulating a Natural Monopoly
cards.definition: Some services are cheapest when one network provides them - a rail line, a water system - so competition cannot discipline the price. Economists call this a natural monopoly. Market economies usually respond with regulation instead of competition: a public commission sets or reviews rates, requires equal treatment of customers, and demands reports. The trade-off is documented on both sides. Regulation limits the abuse of a captive market, but a commission can also be slow, captured, or simply wrong about costs.
cards.example: The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 made railroads the first industry under federal regulation. Farmers on branch lines had faced 1 carrier, rebates for large shippers, and higher rates for short hauls than long ones. The act required 'just and reasonable' rates, banned rebates and short-haul discrimination, and created a 5-member Interstate Commerce Commission. Its own contradictory terms made it only partly effective.

cards.title: Business Births and Deaths
cards.definition: A market economy is constantly reshuffled. New establishments open, old ones close, and jobs are created at some firms while they disappear at others. This churn is how resources move from uses people value less to uses they value more; a closing is often the other side of an opening elsewhere. Statistical agencies track it because the pace of entry and exit says a great deal about competition and about how quickly an economy adapts.
cards.example: The Census Bureau's Business Dynamics Statistics measure exactly this churn: establishment births and deaths, firm startups and shutdowns, and job creation and destruction, published every year for the United States from 1978 through 2023 and broken out by industry, firm size, and firm age. The net change in employment at a location is what a headline jobs number shows; the gross flows underneath it are far larger.

cards.title: When Competition Is Suspended
cards.definition: Because competition is what holds prices down in a market economy, suspending it has predictable effects. If firms in an industry are allowed - or required - to agree on prices, wages, and output, the result looks like a cartel: higher prices, less production, and barriers against newcomers. The United States ran this experiment during the Great Depression, and historians and economists generally document that the codes raised prices and did little to speed recovery.
cards.example: The National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933 suspended the antitrust laws and asked industries to write 'codes of fair competition.' More than 500 codes fixed prices and wages, set production quotas, and restricted entry. Firms displayed a Blue Eagle emblem to show they participated. In May 1935 the Supreme Court struck down the compulsory codes, and the National Archives notes that by raising prices they had made conditions worse.

cards.title: Price Controls
cards.definition: A price control is a legal limit on what a price may be: a ceiling holds it below the market-clearing level, a floor holds it above. Because prices carry information and incentives, a binding control does not remove the pressure that was moving the price; it changes how the pressure shows up. A ceiling produces shortages, queues, and quality cuts. A floor produces surpluses that someone must store, destroy, or subsidize. Controls can pause measured inflation without touching its cause.
cards.example: The Nixon administration imposed wage and price controls in 3 phases between 1971 and 1974, during a period when consumer inflation climbed from a little over 1 percent a year in 1964 to more than 14 percent in 1980. Federal Reserve History records that the controls only temporarily slowed price increases while worsening shortages, particularly of food and energy.

topics.name: Mixed Economies
topics.summary: The roles governments take on inside market systems: measuring output, running enterprises, building infrastructure, managing money, and setting rules for finance and labor.

cards.title: What a Mixed Economy Is
cards.definition: Nearly every real economy is mixed: private markets allocate most goods, while government taxes, spends, regulates, and sometimes produces. Economists describe the mix along a spectrum rather than as two boxes. One way to see the government's weight is in the national accounts, which add up spending by households, businesses, government, and foreign buyers of exports, then subtract imports. Government purchases are one of those components, and they rise or fall with policy choices as well as with the economy.
cards.example: The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that real U.S. GDP grew at a 1.5 percent annual rate in the second quarter of 2026, after 2.1 percent in the first. Consumer spending, exports, and investment rose; government spending fell and partly offset them. The release treats the public sector as one line item among several, which is exactly what a mixed economy looks like in the data.

cards.title: Public Enterprise
cards.definition: A public enterprise is a business owned by government that sells goods or services, often in electricity, water, transport, or postal delivery. Mixed economies use them where private investors will not build at the needed scale, where a network serves a whole region, or where a legislature wants prices or coverage that a private owner would not choose. The documented trade-offs run both ways: broad access and long horizons on one side, weaker cost discipline and political control on the other.
cards.example: The Tennessee Valley Authority was created as a federal corporation on May 18, 1933 to control floods, improve navigation, and generate electricity across a 7-state region. The National Archives describes it as the largest public power company in the United States, with 29 hydroelectric dams, 3 nuclear plants, more than 27,000 megawatts of capacity, and over 16,000 miles of transmission lines serving about 80,000 square miles.

cards.title: Public Infrastructure
cards.definition: Roads, bridges, ports, and water systems are infrastructure: long-lived assets that many users share and that private firms rarely build on their own at national scale, because tolling every user is hard and the benefits spill over to people who never pay. Mixed economies fund much of it publicly, often through earmarked taxes on the users. The choice of where to build then shapes private decisions for decades - where firms locate, where housing is built, which towns grow.
cards.example: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of June 29, 1956 authorized a 41,000-mile Interstate System and $25 billion for fiscal years 1957 through 1969, funded by higher federal taxes on motor fuel, tires, trucks, and buses. The National Archives notes that the network reshaped American settlement around the automobile, cutting through some urban neighborhoods and bypassing small towns along older routes.

cards.title: A Central Bank
cards.definition: A central bank is a public institution that issues the currency, acts as banker to commercial banks, and steadies the financial system in a panic by lending when private lenders will not. Money itself is a shared standard, so even market-oriented economies treat it as a public good rather than leaving it to individual banks. Creating a central bank is a deliberate choice about the mix: it puts one part of the economy under a public authority while leaving lending and deposit-taking largely private.
cards.example: The United States was the only major financial power without a central bank when the Panic of 1907 forced the government to rely on private financiers. Congress created an 18-member National Monetary Commission in 1908, debated a banker-led plan, and in December 1913 passed the Federal Reserve Act instead: a system of regional Reserve Banks overseen by a board in Washington.

cards.title: Bank Rules and Deposit Insurance
cards.definition: Banks sit at the center of a mixed economy's payment system, so their failures spread further than an ordinary firm's. Governments respond with rules on what banks may do and with deposit insurance, a public guarantee that small depositors are repaid if a bank fails. Insurance stops runs but weakens depositors' reason to watch their bank, which is why it is paired with supervision and limits on risk-taking. How tight those limits should be has been argued over for nearly a century.
cards.example: The Banking Act of 1933, signed June 16, 1933, separated commercial banking from securities dealing - a bank could earn no more than 10 percent of its income from securities - and created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, funded by a pool collected from banks. The separation was uncontroversial in 1933; the restrictions on bank-securities affiliations were repealed in 1999.

cards.title: Rules for the Labor Market
cards.definition: Labor is bought and sold in markets, but mixed economies set the rules of that market: who may organize, how disputes are settled, minimum standards for pay and hours. The economic argument for such rules is that individual workers and large employers do not bargain from equal positions and that some outcomes - unsafe conditions, child labor - impose costs others bear. The documented trade-off is that rules also raise employers’ costs and can shift jobs elsewhere.
cards.example: The National Labor Relations Act of July 5, 1935 guaranteed private-sector workers the right to form unions and bargain collectively, and created a 5-member National Labor Relations Board, assisted by 33 regional directors, to run union elections and rule on unfair labor practices. The Supreme Court upheld the law in 1937, and union membership surged in the years that followed.

cards.title: Protective Regulation
cards.definition: Protective regulation restricts what may be sold or how it may be produced - product safety, working conditions, pollution limits. In a mixed economy it exists because some costs of production fall on people outside the transaction, and because buyers cannot easily see every risk. Its reach is contested in law as well as economics: a rule must be authorized by some power the government actually has, and early U.S. attempts were struck down on exactly that ground.
cards.example: The 1900 census counted roughly 2 million children working in mills, mines, fields, and factories. The Keating-Owen Act of 1916 barred interstate sale of goods from factories employing children under 14, from mines employing children under 16, and from any workplace where children under 16 worked nights or more than 8 hours. The Supreme Court voided it in 1918 as beyond the commerce power.

cards.title: Public Investment in People
cards.definition: Governments in mixed economies also spend on human capital - schooling, training, health - on the argument that an educated worker raises the productivity of others and pays taxes for decades, so the return is not captured by the student alone. Economists call this a positive spillover. Measuring the payoff is hard because the people who receive such benefits differ from those who do not, and because the gains arrive slowly and show up partly in other people’s incomes.
cards.example: The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, the G.I. Bill, paid tuition and living costs for veterans. Within 7 years about 8 million had used its education benefits; by 1956 the education portion had cost $14.5 billion, and 4.3 million home loans worth $33 billion had been guaranteed by 1955. The share of Americans holding a bachelor's degree rose from 4.6 percent in 1945 to 25 percent 50 years later.

topics.name: Planned Economies
topics.summary: How central planning allocated resources through quotas and plans, what administered prices and rationing did to supply, and how planned economies moved toward markets.

cards.title: What Central Planning Is
cards.definition: Every economy must answer three questions: what to produce, how to produce it, and who receives it. A command or planned economy answers them through a central authority rather than through prices. The state owns most productive assets, planners set output targets for factories and farms, and prices are administered rather than discovered in exchange. Economists contrast this with a market economy along a spectrum; real systems have mixed the two, and the balance has moved over time.
cards.example: In a 1997 speech titled 'The Embrace of Free Markets', the Federal Reserve chairman described the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 as a natural experiment between the 2 systems: planned economies, lacking price signals, produced surpluses of goods nobody wanted beside shortages of goods people needed, and used 5 to 7 times as much energy per unit of output as Western economies. His verdict on rigid central planning: unequivocally negative.

cards.title: Quotas and the Five-Year Plan
cards.definition: The working tool of a planned economy is the plan: a multi-year document that sets output targets for each sector and passes them down as quotas to individual enterprises. Managers are judged on meeting the quota, not on cost or on whether anyone wants the product. Because the targets are set from above with little information from below, they can be unrealistic, and because everything is scheduled at once, a shortfall in one input ripples through every plant that depends on it.
cards.example: The Soviet Union's First Five-Year Plan, adopted in 1928, called for a 250 percent increase in overall industrial output and a 330 percent expansion of heavy industry. All industry and services were nationalized, managers received predetermined quotas from central planners, and trade unions became instruments for raising output. The Library of Congress exhibit notes that the targets were unrealistic and that serious problems soon followed.

cards.title: Collectivization
cards.definition: Collectivization replaces individual farms with large state-directed collectives. The economic logic planners gave was scale and control: pooled land and machinery would raise yields, and the state could take the grain surplus to feed cities and pay for industry. The record shows the reverse in the Soviet case. Removing ownership removed the incentive to produce, resistance was met with force, and output collapsed. It is the clearest historical illustration of what happens when property rights in food are abolished.
cards.example: The First Five-Year Plan called for collectivizing 20 percent of peasant households; by 1940 roughly 97 percent had been collectivized and private property nearly eliminated. About 1 million wealthier peasant households - some 5 million people - were deported and never heard from again, and forced collectivization produced a catastrophic famine in 1932 and 1933.

cards.title: Shortages and Queues
cards.definition: When a price is held below the level at which supply equals demand, more is wanted than is offered, and the gap is a shortage. In a market that shortage pushes the price up until some buyers drop out and sellers add supply. A planned economy fixes prices by decree, so the adjustment cannot happen through price. It happens instead through waiting: queues, waiting lists, connections, and informal markets at higher prices. Time, not money, becomes the rationing device.
cards.example: The St. Louis Fed's primer on prices describes the mechanism with a rent-control example: at a ceiling below the market rent, the number of apartments renters want exceeds the number landlords supply, and a shortage results. Administered prices in a planned economy are ceilings on nearly everything at once, so the queue for 1 good was matched by queues for dozens of others.

cards.title: Wartime Rationing
cards.definition: Rationing is planned allocation inside an otherwise market economy. Instead of letting prices rise to clear a scarce good, the government issues coupons that cap how much each household may buy, so that supply is divided by rule rather than by ability to pay. It is usually paired with price controls and public appeals to conserve. Wartime governments accepted the costs - black markets, administration, mismatched allocations - to steer materials to the military and to spread the burden.
cards.example: During the Second World War the United States rationed gasoline, rubber, sugar, butter, and meat. National Archives posters from 1943 urged civilians to share rides and to save waste fats for explosives, explaining that shortages existed because the goods were going to the troops. The War Production Board's chairman put the priority bluntly: the military would get 'astronomical quantities of everything.'

cards.title: From Plan to Market
cards.definition: Transition is the shift from a planned economy to a market one: freeing prices, allowing private ownership, opening trade, and building the institutions - courts, banks, tax systems - that markets take for granted. The sequence matters and was argued over fiercely. Freeing prices first exposes how far administered prices had been held below cost, so measured inflation jumps. Output usually falls before it recovers, because old supply chains break faster than new ones form.
cards.example: The IMF's 2000 review of the former communist economies found that output fell on average 40 percent from the start of transition before bottoming out. Early on, inflation averaged 450 percent a year in Central and Eastern Europe, nearly 900 percent in the Baltics, and over 1,000 percent in the Commonwealth of Independent States; by 1998 it was in single digits in the first two groups and around 30 percent in the third.

cards.title: China's Reform Path
cards.definition: Not every move away from planning happened at once. A gradual path keeps state ownership in parts of the economy while allowing markets to grow alongside: farmers keep what they produce above a quota, private and foreign firms enter, prices are freed sector by sector. Economists document very large gains in output and living standards from this route, together with imbalances - heavy reliance on investment and exports, environmental damage, and a state role that remains larger than in most market economies.
cards.example: The World Bank reports that since 1978, when China's reform and opening period began, GDP growth has averaged over 9 percent a year, lifting almost 800 million people out of extreme poverty; by 2020 extreme poverty had been eliminated. In 2024, however, 15.2 percent of the population still lived on less than $8.30 a day at 2021 purchasing-power parity, a higher benchmark the Bank uses to compare countries.

cards.title: Privatization Paths
cards.definition: Privatization moves state assets into private hands, and how it is done shapes what follows. Rapid methods - vouchers handed to every citizen, or quick sales to insiders - transfer ownership fast but often leave firms without owners able or willing to restructure them. Gradual sales to strategic buyers take longer and can be more transparent. Economists studying the 1990s found that speed alone did not deliver better firms; the quality of ownership and of the surrounding institutions mattered more.
cards.example: The IMF's 2000 assessment contrasted the paths. Voucher assets handed to millions of citizens were often sold on and consolidated in investment funds that did little restructuring; Russia's loans-for-shares scheme was non-transparent and systematically excluded foreign investors. Hungary's gradual approach, by contrast, appeared more conducive to genuine restructuring of enterprises. By 2000 several Central European and Baltic economies were candidates to join the European Union.

topics.name: Welfare-State Models
topics.summary: How welfare states pool risk and redistribute income through social insurance and assistance, how poverty and coverage are measured, and how the programs are financed.

cards.title: What a Welfare State Is
cards.definition: A welfare state is a market economy in which government takes responsibility for protecting people against major risks to income: old age, illness, disability, unemployment, and poverty. The World Bank groups the tools into three pillars - social assistance, paid from general taxes to people in need; social insurance, financed by contributions and paid out when an insured event occurs; and labor-market programs that help people find or keep work. Countries differ mainly in how large each pillar is and who qualifies.
cards.example: Coverage is far from universal worldwide. The World Bank's 2025 State of Social Protection report counts 2 billion people without adequate protection, and 3 out of 4 people in low-income countries without basic protection. The Bank reports $29.5 billion in social protection financing as of April 2025 and estimates that each dollar transferred to poor families generates about $2.50 of activity in the local economy.

cards.title: Universal and Means-Tested Programs
cards.definition: Welfare programs differ in who qualifies. A universal or categorical program pays everyone in a group - all people over a certain age, all children - regardless of income. A means-tested program pays only those whose income or assets fall below a line. Universal programs are simple to run and widely supported but expensive; means-tested programs cost less and target need, but require applications and checks, and can discourage earning more because benefits fall as income rises. Most welfare states use both.
cards.example: The Social Security Amendments of 1965, signed July 30, 1965, created both kinds at once: Medicare, hospital insurance for everyone aged 65 and older, financed by a tax on earnings matched by employers, and Medicaid, health coverage for people with limited income, funded jointly by states and the federal government. Nearly 20 million people enrolled in the program's first 3 years. In 1950 only 1 in 8 older Americans had health insurance.

cards.title: Measuring Poverty
cards.definition: A poverty line is an income threshold below which a household is counted as poor. The line and the income definition both matter. The official U.S. measure, in use since the 1960s, compares pre-tax money income with a threshold that varies by family size. The Supplemental Poverty Measure, published since 2011, adds the value of food and housing assistance and refundable tax credits, subtracts taxes, work costs, and medical spending, and adjusts thresholds for local housing costs. The two measures can move differently.
cards.example: For 2024 the Census Bureau reported an official poverty rate of 10.6 percent, down 0.4 percentage points, with 35.9 million people below the line. The Supplemental Poverty Measure rate was 12.9 percent, statistically unchanged from 2023. Under that measure Social Security was the largest single antipoverty program, moving 28.7 million people above the threshold in 2024.

cards.definition: Countries organize health coverage in different ways: a single public insurer paid from taxes; compulsory insurance through many funds; or a mix in which most working-age people are covered through employers, older and low-income people through public programs, and some buy coverage directly. Each model trades off different things - universality, choice, cost control, and how the bill is split between taxes, premiums, and payments at the point of care. The United States runs the mixed model.

cards.title: Unemployment Insurance as a Stabilizer
cards.definition: Unemployment insurance pays cash benefits to workers who lose a job through no fault of their own, funded by payroll taxes on employers. Beyond protecting the individual, it is an automatic stabilizer: payments rise in a recession without any new vote, putting spending into the economy exactly when private demand is falling, and shrink again as people return to work. The documented trade-off is that generous or long benefits can lengthen job searches, which is why eligibility and duration are limited.
cards.example: There is no single federal program. Each state runs its own unemployment insurance system and pays its own claims, setting eligibility rules and benefit levels; many require that a worker earned at least a set amount within the previous 12 to 24 months. Claims are generally filed in the state where the person worked, not the state where they live, which matters for remote and cross-border workers.

cards.title: Extreme Poverty Worldwide
cards.definition: Welfare-state debates in rich countries sit against a different global picture. The World Bank counts a person as extremely poor if they live on less than a fixed daily amount, measured in purchasing-power terms so that the line buys the same basket everywhere. Growth has done most of the work of reducing that count, and formal safety nets remain thin in the poorest countries. Economists document that growth alone is not enough: infrastructure, schooling, and institutions determine who climbs out.
cards.example: Between 1990 and 2025 the number of people in extreme poverty fell from around 2.3 billion to 831 million, each living on less than $3 a day, driven largely by broad-based growth in East Asia and South Asia. Progress slowed substantially in the decade to 2025. In 2024 an estimated 412 million children aged 17 or younger lived below that line, and extreme poverty is increasingly concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and conflict-affected places.

cards.title: Financing Social Insurance
cards.definition: Social insurance is paid for mainly by earmarked payroll taxes, split between employee and employer, rather than from general revenue. The design ties benefits to contributions, which is what makes the program insurance rather than assistance and gives it durable political support. It also means the tax falls on wages: economists generally find that the employer share is largely borne by workers through lower pay over time. Rates that start low tend to rise as the covered population ages and benefits mature.
cards.example: The Social Security Act, signed August 14, 1935, created old-age insurance funded by a tax on employees’ wages matched by an equal excise tax on employers. The employee rate began at 1 percent for 1937 through 1939 and was scheduled to reach 3 percent by 1949. The same act appropriated $49,750,000 for old-age assistance and $24,750,000 for aid to dependent children for fiscal year 1936.

cards.title: Income Before and After Taxes and Transfers
cards.definition: How much a welfare state redistributes depends on which income is measured. Market income is what households earn before government acts. Adding cash benefits and refundable credits, then subtracting taxes, gives post-tax, post-transfer income. Inequality measured on the second is lower than on the first, and the gap between the two is one way to size a country's redistribution. In-kind benefits such as health coverage are usually left out of both, which understates what low-income households receive.
cards.example: The Census Bureau's headline income figures use pre-tax money income and exclude in-kind transfers: median household income was $83,730 in 2024, not statistically different from 2023, and the Gini index of inequality was unchanged. The same report publishes post-tax income and inequality estimates separately in an appendix, so readers can compare the two definitions for the same households and year.

packs.name: Personal Finance
packs.summary: The mechanics behind a paycheck, a car or home purchase, a credit score, and a savings balance: what the forms and numbers mean and how time changes them.

topics.name: Paychecks & Taxes
topics.summary: What comes out of a paycheck and why: withholding, the W-4 and W-2, payroll taxes, filing status, marginal brackets, refunds, and the extra rules for self-employment.

cards.title: Withholding
cards.definition: Withholding is income tax taken out of each paycheck by the employer and sent to the government on the worker's behalf. It is a prepayment, not the final bill. How much is withheld depends on two things: how much the worker earns and the information the worker gives the employer on Form W-4. Employers are required by law to withhold, and the same rule applies to Social Security and Medicare taxes. Tax can also be withheld from pensions, bonuses, and commissions.
cards.example: A worker paid every 2 weeks receives 26 paychecks a year, and each one carries a slice of the year's expected income tax. If the total withheld over the year is more than the tax actually owed on the return, the difference comes back as a refund; if it is less, the worker owes the balance at filing time. The IRS offers an online estimator to check the setting during the year.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Internal Revenue Service

cards.title: Form W-4
cards.definition: Form W-4, the Employee's Withholding Certificate, is the form a worker gives an employer so that the right amount of federal income tax is withheld. It tells the employer about filing status, other jobs in the household, dependents, and any extra amount to withhold per paycheck. It is not filed with a tax return; the employer keeps it. The IRS suggests reviewing it each year and whenever circumstances change, because the form only reflects what the worker last reported.
cards.example: Two common triggers are a marriage and a second job. A couple who both work and both leave their W-4 set for a single earner with 1 job can end up under-withheld, because each employer assumes its paycheck is the only one. Filing a new W-4 within a few weeks of the change corrects the estimate for the remaining paychecks of the year.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Form W-2
cards.definition: Form W-2, the Wage and Tax Statement, is the employer's annual report of what it paid an employee and what it withheld. Every employer that pays wages must file one for each employee from whom income, Social Security, or Medicare tax was withheld, or who would have had tax withheld absent an exemption. Copies go to the worker and to the government, so the numbers on a return can be matched against the employer's report.
cards.example: Someone who held 3 jobs during a year receives 3 W-2 forms, 1 from each employer, and adds the wage and withholding boxes together on the return. If an employer discovers an error after issuing the form, it files a corrected statement, Form W-2c, so that the worker’s record and the return can be matched. A missing form is requested from the employer, not the IRS.

cards.title: Payroll Taxes: Social Security and Medicare
cards.definition: Alongside income tax, paychecks carry payroll taxes under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act. Two separate taxes apply: one funds Social Security's old-age, survivors, and disability insurance and one funds Medicare's hospital insurance. Each is paid half by the employee and half by the employer, at flat rates. Only the Social Security portion has a wage base limit, an annual ceiling on earnings subject to the tax; Medicare tax applies to all covered wages, with an additional rate above a high threshold.
cards.example: The rates published by the IRS are 6.2 percent each for employee and employer for Social Security, 12.4 percent combined, and 1.45 percent each for Medicare, 2.9 percent combined. For earnings in 2026 the Social Security wage base limit is $184,500. An Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9 percent is withheld on wages above $200,000 in a calendar year, with no employer match.

cards.title: Filing Status
cards.definition: Filing status is the category a taxpayer files under, and it sets the standard deduction, the bracket thresholds, and eligibility for some credits. The IRS lists five: single; married filing jointly; married filing separately; head of household; and qualifying surviving spouse. Status is generally determined by marital situation on the last day of the year, so a December wedding counts for the whole year. When more than one status fits, the taxpayer may choose the one that produces the lower tax.
cards.example: Head of household is for an unmarried person who paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for themselves and a qualifying dependent; it carries a larger standard deduction than single. Qualifying surviving spouse applies for up to 2 years after a spouse's death when there is a dependent child. The IRS notes that most married couples pay less by filing jointly than separately.

cards.title: Tax Brackets Are Marginal
cards.definition: Federal income tax is charged in layers called brackets. Each bracket's rate applies only to the slice of taxable income that falls inside it, not to the whole amount. Moving into a higher bracket therefore raises the tax on the next dollar earned, not on the dollars already taxed at lower rates. The rate on the last dollar is the marginal rate; total tax divided by total income is the average rate, and it is always lower than the marginal rate.
cards.example: For tax year 2025 a single filer's first $11,925 of taxable income is taxed at 10 percent, the next slice up to $48,475 at 12 percent, and the slice up to $103,350 at 22 percent. An illustrative single filer with $60,000 of taxable income owes $1,192.50 plus $4,386 plus $2,535.50, about $8,114 in total: a 22 percent marginal rate but an average rate near 13.5 percent.

cards.title: Refunds and Balances Due
cards.definition: A refund is not a bonus; it is the return of tax that was prepaid through withholding or estimated payments beyond what the year's return shows is owed. A balance due is the reverse. Both are settled when the return is filed. Refunds can be reduced to pay past-due federal taxes, child support, or certain other debts before the remainder is sent, and returns that claim some credits are held by law until mid-February so the claims can be checked.
cards.example: The IRS describes typical timing: about 3 weeks after an electronically filed return and 6 or more weeks after a mailed one, with delays when a return needs correction or review. Refund status can be checked 24 hours after e-filing a current-year return, or 4 weeks after mailing a paper return. A large refund every year means more was withheld than needed all year long.

cards.title: Self-Employment Tax
cards.definition: Someone who works for themselves has no employer to withhold tax or to pay the employer half of Social Security and Medicare. Self-employment tax fills that gap: it is both halves combined, calculated on net earnings using Schedule SE and paid with the return, usually through quarterly estimated payments. Because an employee never sees the employer share, the combined rate looks large by comparison. The law offsets part of it by letting the self-employed deduct the employer-equivalent half when computing adjusted gross income.
cards.example: The self-employment tax rate is 15.3 percent: 12.4 percent for Social Security plus 2.9 percent for Medicare. It applies once net self-employment earnings reach $400 or more in a year. For 2024, the IRS page states, only the first $168,600 of combined wages and net earnings was subject to the Social Security part, while the Medicare part applied to all of it, with an extra 0.9 percent above a filing-status threshold.

topics.name: Buying a Car or a Home
topics.summary: How auto loans, leases, and mortgages are priced and disclosed, and the mechanics of negative equity, down payments, PMI, the Loan Estimate, escrow, and renting versus owning.

cards.title: Reading the Loan Disclosure
cards.definition: Before an auto loan is signed, the federal Truth in Lending Act requires the lender or dealer to hand over a disclosure that states the loan's cost in a standard way. Four numbers matter most: the annual percentage rate, which folds interest and mandatory fees into one yearly percentage; the finance charge, the total interest and fees over the life of the loan; the amount financed; and the total of payments. The monthly payment alone hides the last three.
cards.example: An illustrative $25,000 loan at a 7 percent rate costs about $599 a month over 48 months, a finance charge near $3,735 and a total of payments around $28,735. The same loan stretched to 72 months costs about $426 a month - but the finance charge rises to roughly $5,688 and the total to about $30,688. The disclosure puts those totals side by side; the sales pitch usually does not.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

cards.title: Leasing Versus Buying
cards.definition: A lease buys the right to use a car for a set time and a set number of miles; a loan buys the car. Lease payments are usually lower than loan payments on the same vehicle because the lessee pays only for the depreciation expected during the term, plus a rent charge, taxes, and fees, and hands the car back at the end unless the contract allows a purchase. The lessee also carries obligations a buyer does not: mileage caps, wear standards, and early-termination charges.
cards.example: The FTC notes that most standard leases cap mileage at 15,000 a year or less; a higher cap raises the payment because the car loses more value, and exceeding it brings an added fee at return. Someone who drives 20,000 miles a year and keeps cars for 8 years faces very different costs under the two contracts, even when the first year’s payments look similar.
cards.disclaimer: Educational content only. EconByte does not provide financial, investment, or tax advice.

source.organization: Federal Trade Commission, Consumer Advice

cards.title: Negative Equity
cards.definition: Negative equity means owing more on a car loan than the car is worth. It arises because a new car loses value quickly while a long loan pays down principal slowly, and it grows with small down payments and rolled-in fees. It surfaces at trade-in time: a dealer may offer to fold the shortfall into the next loan, which raises the new balance, lengthens the term, or increases the payment, and starts the next loan already underwater.
cards.example: An illustrative driver owes $18,000 on a car worth $15,000 as a trade-in: $3,000 of negative equity. Rolling it into a $25,000 purchase means financing $28,000 for a car worth $25,000 on day 1. The CFPB's guidance is to learn the loan's payoff amount, which can differ from the statement balance, and to confirm about a week after the new deal that the old loan was actually paid off.

cards.title: Fixed and Adjustable Mortgages
cards.definition: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate, and therefore the same principal-and-interest payment, for the life of the loan. An adjustable-rate mortgage starts with a rate that holds for an introductory period and then resets at regular intervals. The new rate is an index - a broad measure of market interest rates - plus a margin the lender sets, subject to caps that limit how far the rate can move at each reset and over the loan's life.
cards.example: Suppose an illustrative adjustable loan starts at 5 percent for 5 years with a margin of 2.5 percentage points. If the index stands at 4 percent at the first reset, the new rate is 6.5 percent - unless a cap limits the jump. The CFPB cautions against assuming a sale or refinance will come before the reset, since home values and personal finances can change.

cards.title: Down Payments and PMI
cards.definition: The down payment is the part of the price paid in cash; the mortgage covers the rest. The ratio between them changes the loan's terms. On a conventional loan with less than 20 percent down, lenders generally require private mortgage insurance, a policy the borrower pays for but that protects the lender if payments stop. PMI is charged as a monthly premium, an up-front premium at closing, or both, and it appears on the Loan Estimate and the Closing Disclosure.
cards.example: On an illustrative $300,000 home, 10 percent down is $30,000 and leaves a $270,000 loan that would ordinarily carry PMI; 20 percent down is $60,000 and a $240,000 loan without it. The CFPB notes that some lenders offer low-down-payment loans without PMI in exchange for a higher interest rate, which can cost more or less than PMI depending on how long the borrower keeps the loan.

cards.title: The Loan Estimate
cards.definition: The Loan Estimate is a standardized 3-page form a mortgage lender must deliver within 3 business days of receiving an application. Every lender uses the same layout, which is the point: it lets a borrower line up offers from different lenders and compare the interest rate, monthly payment, estimated taxes and insurance, and total closing costs. It also flags features worth knowing about, such as a prepayment penalty or negative amortization. Receiving one does not mean the loan is approved.
cards.example: A borrower who applies to 3 lenders on the same day can expect 3 Loan Estimates by the end of the third business day and can compare them page by page. Closing costs include lender fees, third-party charges, and prepaid items such as property taxes and homeowners insurance. The form shows what the lender expects to offer; the final figures arrive on the Closing Disclosure.

cards.title: Escrow Accounts
cards.definition: An escrow account, called an impound account in some states, is a holding account the mortgage servicer runs to pay property taxes and insurance premiums on the borrower's behalf. A share of each monthly payment goes into it, and the servicer pays the bills when they fall due, once or twice a year. Many lenders require escrow so that the taxes and insurance protecting their collateral are certain to be paid. Because those bills change, the escrow portion of the payment is recalculated each year.
cards.example: If an illustrative home carries $3,600 a year in property taxes and $1,200 in homeowners insurance, the escrow share of the payment is $400 a month on top of principal and interest. A borrower without escrow must set that $4,800 aside alone. The CFPB warns that if taxes or insurance go unpaid, the lender may buy force-placed insurance, typically more expensive, and bill the borrower.

cards.title: Renting Versus Owning
cards.definition: The rent-or-own question is a comparison of two cost streams under uncertainty. Owning builds equity - the home's value minus the mortgage balance - but slowly at first, because early payments are mostly interest, and equity also moves with market prices. It carries transaction costs at purchase and sale, plus maintenance and repairs. Renting avoids those costs and preserves the option to move, at the price of building no equity. Calculators that compare the two depend heavily on assumed price growth.
cards.example: The CFPB's guide notes that someone who sells within the first few years may end up with no more equity than they started with after paying the transaction costs, and that when prices fell between 2007 and 2012 many owners lost some or all of their equity. Owners also bear repairs a landlord would otherwise cover, so the comparison must include more than a rent check against a mortgage payment.

topics.summary: What builds a credit score, how to read and correct a credit report, how identity theft and imposter scams work, and what regulators report about fraud losses.

cards.title: What Moves a Score
cards.definition: A credit score is a prediction of repayment built from a credit report, and each scoring model weighs a handful of behaviors. Payment history counts most: paying every account on time as agreed. Next is utilization, how much of available credit is in use; models read balances near the limit as strain. Length of history helps because it gives the model more evidence. Recent applications for new credit count against a score because they can signal financial trouble.
cards.example: The CFPB relays a common guideline: keep balances at no more than 30 percent of total credit limits. Closing 2 unused cards can therefore lower a score if the same balances now sit on 1 card near its limit. Carrying a balance is not required; paying in full each month produces the strongest scores and the lowest interest cost.

cards.title: Free Credit Reports
cards.definition: A credit report is the file a credit reporting company keeps on a person's accounts and payment history, and scores are computed from it. Federal law gives everyone the right to a free copy of their report from each of the 3 nationwide credit reporting companies once every 12 months, obtained through the single official website or phone line set up for that purpose. Additional free reports are available after a denial of credit, insurance, or employment based on a report.
cards.example: Because the 3 reports can be ordered separately, one approach the CFPB describes is to request 1 every 4 months to watch the file across the year. Beyond the free copies, a company may charge no more than $14.50 for a report. A denial notice gives 60 days to request a free report from the company named in it.

cards.title: Disputing an Error
cards.definition: Errors in a credit report can lower a score and raise borrowing costs, and federal law gives the consumer a right to dispute them. A dispute goes to the credit reporting company, in writing with copies of supporting documents, and often also to the company that supplied the information, called the furnisher. The reporting company must investigate, forward the dispute and evidence to the furnisher, and report the result back; it may decline only disputes it reasonably finds frivolous.
cards.example: The CFPB's checklist for a mailed dispute: full contact information, each item in question with its account number, a clear explanation of why it is wrong, a request to remove or correct it, a copy of the report page with the items circled, and copies - never originals - of documents. The same letter can go to all 3 companies if all 3 show the error, and certified mail with a return receipt creates a dated record.

cards.title: How Long Information Stays
cards.definition: Credit reporting companies may report most negative information for a limited time, after which it must drop off the report even though the company may keep it on file. Positive information can stay longer, and an on-time history can remain after an account is closed, which helps scores that reward long histories. No one can lawfully remove accurate negative information early; companies that charge fees to 'repair' credit cannot do what a consumer can do alone for free, which is dispute actual errors.
cards.example: The general limit is 7 years for late payments and most other negative items, and up to 10 years for bankruptcies; a judgment can stay 7 years or until the statute of limitations runs out, whichever is longer. The limits do not apply when a report is used for a job paying more than $75,000 a year or for credit or life insurance above $150,000.

cards.title: Identity Theft
cards.definition: Identity theft is the use of someone's personal or financial information - a Social Security number, a card or account number, a date of birth - without permission, usually to open accounts, file claims, or make purchases in their name. The information is taken in mundane ways: a stolen wallet, discarded statements, card skimmers on pumps and machines, phishing messages, public Wi-Fi, and details posted on social media. The victim often learns of it only from the aftermath.
cards.example: Warning signs USAGov lists include debt-collection calls for accounts never opened, unfamiliar accounts on a credit report, and mail that stops arriving. Recovery runs through the FTC's identity theft site and the 3 credit reporting companies, where fraud alerts and a freeze can be placed. Someone whose information was used to file a false tax return completes IRS Form 14039, an affidavit that invalidates the fraudulent return.

cards.title: Credit Freezes and Fraud Alerts
cards.definition: A credit freeze locks a credit file so that no new credit account can be opened in the person's name - including by the person - until the freeze is temporarily lifted. It is free, does not affect scores, and can be placed by anyone at any time. A fraud alert is lighter: it leaves the file visible but tells lenders to verify identity before granting new credit. Freezes must be placed with each reporting company; an alert placed with one is passed to the others.
cards.example: The FTC describes 3 kinds of alert. An initial fraud alert lasts 1 year and can be renewed by anyone who suspects identity theft. An extended alert lasts 7 years, requires an identity theft or police report, and removes the person from prescreened credit and insurance offers for 5 years. An active-duty alert for servicemembers removes them from those lists for 2 years.

cards.title: Imposter Scams and Fraud Losses
cards.definition: An imposter scam is fraud by impersonation: the caller, texter, or emailer claims to be a government agency, a bank, a utility, a familiar company, or a relative in trouble, and uses that borrowed authority to extract money or personal information. The FTC collects fraud reports from consumers nationwide and publishes the totals each year. Reported losses understate the real figure, since many victims never report, but the pattern across categories and payment methods is informative.
cards.example: For 2024 the FTC reported more than $12.5 billion in losses to fraud, up 25 percent from the prior year, from about 2.6 million fraud reports. Imposter scams were the most commonly reported category, with $2.95 billion lost, and losses to government imposters alone reached $789 million. Investment scams cost the most, $5.7 billion. The share of reporters who lost money rose from 27 percent in 2023 to 38 percent in 2024.

cards.title: Ponzi Schemes
cards.definition: A Ponzi scheme is an investment fraud that pays earlier participants with money collected from later ones, while claiming the payments are returns on a real strategy. Little or nothing is actually invested, so the scheme depends on a constant inflow of new money; it collapses when recruiting slows or many participants try to withdraw at once. The warning signs the SEC lists match the mechanism: unusually steady returns in all market conditions, unregistered investments, unlicensed sellers, and strategies too secret or complex to explain.
cards.example: The name comes from Charles Ponzi, who took in investors in the 1920s with a postage-stamp arbitrage story. The SEC's Office of Investor Education notes that promoters often push participants to roll over rather than cash out by offering still higher returns for staying in, and that trouble receiving payments or errors on account statements are signs that funds are not being invested as promised.

cards.title: Principal and Interest
cards.definition: Principal is the money deposited or borrowed; interest is the price paid for its use, expressed as a percentage of principal per year. On a deposit, the bank pays the saver; on a loan, the borrower pays the lender. Simple interest is computed on the original principal only, so each period earns the same amount. Compound interest is computed on principal plus interest already credited, so each period's earnings are slightly larger than the last. Over long spans the difference becomes large.
cards.example: Under simple interest an illustrative $1,000 at 4 percent earns $40 every year - $400 after 10 years. Under annual compounding the same deposit earns $40 the first year, then $41.60 on $1,040, and so on, reaching about $480 of interest after 10 years. The FDIC's primer puts it plainly: the interest is added to the principal, and the next interest is earned on the new, larger principal.

cards.title: Compound Interest
cards.definition: Compounding is interest earning interest. After the first period, the credited interest joins the principal, and the next period's interest is calculated on the larger sum. Early on the effect is barely visible - a few cents of interest on interest. But the extra amount itself compounds, so growth accelerates over time, and the final balance depends far more on how long the money was left than on the size of any single year's gain. The same mathematics works against a borrower who carries a balance.
cards.example: The SEC's classroom example: $100 earning 5 percent a year becomes $105 after 1 year and $110.25 after 2, the extra 25 cents being interest on the first year's $5. Left alone, the $100 grows to more than $162 after 10 years and to almost $340 after 25 years, without another cent deposited. Nearly all of the later gain is interest on earlier interest.

cards.title: Inflation and Purchasing Power
cards.definition: Inflation is a general rise in prices, which is the same thing as a fall in what a unit of money buys. A savings balance that stays fixed in dollars shrinks in purchasing power every year prices rise. Because it compounds like interest, even a low rate matters over decades. Central banks aim for a low, stable rate so that households and businesses can plan; the U.S. Federal Reserve states its objective as a specific number measured by a specific price index.
cards.example: The Federal Open Market Committee judges that inflation of 2 percent over the longer run, measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with its mandate for price stability and maximum employment. At exactly that pace, prices double in roughly 35 years, so $100 set aside at the start buys about what $50 did.

cards.title: APY: Comparing Rates Fairly
cards.definition: Two accounts can quote the same interest rate and pay different amounts, because one compounds more often. The annual percentage yield, or APY, removes that ambiguity: it is the total interest an account pays over a 365-day year, including the effect of compounding frequency, expressed as a single percentage of the deposit. Federal disclosure rules require banks to state it, so APY - not the nominal rate - is the number that makes savings accounts and certificates of deposit comparable.
cards.example: The rule's own worked example: an account that pays $53.90 of interest in a year on a $1,000 deposit, compounded daily, has an APY of 5.39 percent. By the same arithmetic, an illustrative 4 percent rate compounded monthly yields about 4.07 percent, and compounded daily about 4.08 percent - small gaps on one deposit, but the fair way to rank offers.

cards.title: The Rule of 72
cards.definition: The Rule of 72 is a mental shortcut for compounding: dividing 72 by an annual growth rate gives the approximate number of years for an amount to double. It is an approximation, most accurate for rates in the single digits and steadily less so at higher rates, where it overstates the doubling time. It works in reverse too: dividing 72 by an inflation rate gives roughly how long until money buys half as much. It assumes a constant rate, which real returns rarely deliver.
cards.example: The SEC's classroom material uses 9 percent: 72 divided by 9 is 8, so a sum growing at 9 percent doubles in about 8 years, and the exact answer is also 8.0. At 2 percent the rule gives 36 years against an exact 35. At an illustrative 24 percent - a common credit card rate - the rule says 3 years while the true doubling time is about 3.2, close enough to show how fast a carried balance grows.

cards.title: Savings Measured in Months
cards.definition: A useful way to size a cash reserve is in time rather than dollars: how many months of essential spending it would cover if income stopped. Measured that way, the target scales automatically with a household's costs, and it can be built in steps. The CFPB's guidance ties the amount to the person's own history of unexpected expenses and income swings rather than to a universal figure, and notes that a reserve of any size shortens recovery from a shock and reduces reliance on borrowing.
cards.example: For an illustrative household spending $2,400 a month on essentials, 3 months of runway is $7,200 and 6 months is $14,400. Saving $200 a month reaches the 3-month mark in 36 months; adding part of a tax refund, one of the strategies the CFPB describes, shortens that. The unit is months of time bought, which is why the same dollar total means different things to different households.

cards.title: Time in the Account
cards.definition: Because compounding accelerates, the length of time money stays on deposit matters more than most people expect, and it matters more than modest differences in rate. Two deposits of the same size at the same rate end up far apart if one is left three times as long. The FDIC's primer names the two variables together - the interest rate and time - as the pair that determines how much a balance grows, and it is the second that a saver controls most directly.
cards.example: An illustrative $1,000 at 5 percent a year grows to about $1,629 after 10 years and to about $4,322 after 30. The second 20 years add roughly $2,693 - more than 4 times what the first 10 added - even though the rate never changed. A saver who starts 10 years later and stops at the same date forgoes that later, largest stretch of growth.

cards.title: Real Return
cards.definition: The real return on savings is the interest rate minus the inflation rate: what the balance gains in purchasing power rather than in dollars. A deposit earning less than inflation loses ground even as its balance rises. The FDIC publishes a national deposit rate, the average of what insured banks and credit unions pay on common account types, weighted by each institution's share of deposits, which shows how far typical savings rates sit from the rates on other instruments.
cards.example: As of August 17, 2026 the FDIC's national deposit rate was 0.38 percent for savings accounts, 0.63 percent for money market accounts, and 1.71 percent for 12-month certificates of deposit. Against an illustrative 3 percent inflation rate, a savings balance earning 0.38 percent loses about 2.6 percent of its purchasing power in a year, while the 12-month certificate loses about 1.3 percent.
